blocks.text: The goal is to recognize 13 formats and make defensible validity judgments. Start with the fundamentals; you can mark any section complete in one click and reopen it. blocks.text: A sequence is an ordered string of symbols. DNA uses A, C, G and T; a declared alphabet may also allow ambiguity codes such as N, which means an unspecified nucleotide. Protein sequences use amino-acid letters, so a DNA-only rule cannot judge a declared protein sequence. A sequencing read is an observed sequence; a reference sequence is a named comparison sequence. A file’s syntax does not prove whether its contents are authentic reads or the correct reference. Reference identity includes the assembly/version and sequence names, lengths and, when required, checksums.

blocks.text: A record is one structured entry; a header declares context. Tabs separate fields in the examples below; line breaks separate rows. A format can use a specific missing marker, such as . or *, rather than an empty field. Plain text, compressed text and binary containers are different representations. Compression or an extension such as .bam is a clue; inspect the container or parse the contents to establish its type. An index supports lookup and is separate from the data file.

sections.title: Count bases without an off-by-one error

blocks.text: For an ordinary interval, 0-based half-open [start,end) includes start and excludes end: length = end − start. A 1-based inclusive interval includes both endpoints: length = end − start + 1. The same bases [1,4) in the first convention are [2,4] in the second. For ordinary nonempty intervals, add 1 to a 0-based start to get an inclusive start; the end number stays the same. Individual formats also define special insertion, unknown-coordinate or circular cases; do not override those rules with this ordinary-interval shortcut.

sections.title: Decode a quality symbol using a declared encoding

blocks.text: A per-base quality string assigns one encoded quality symbol to each sequence base. For the modern Phred+33 profile, quality score Q = ASCII code − 33. The encoding is supplied context; historical encodings overlap, so characters alone do not always identify it. Here Q is only decoded as a confidence score: higher is greater stated confidence, and Q=0 can be a legal low-confidence value. Per-base, mapping, genotype and variant quality measure different things and cannot be treated as interchangeable.

sections.title: Match each read base to one quality symbol

blocks.text: Modern unwrapped FASTQ uses four lines per read: @title, sequence, +separator, quality. Under our DNA profile, sequence symbols are A/C/G/T/N; quality symbols are printable ASCII 33–126 using Phred+33. Sequence and quality lengths must match. A repeated title after + is optional. Historical/general FASTQ can wrap sequence and quality over multiple lines; compare concatenated lengths there. @ and + can also be quality symbols, so do not split wrapped files merely whenever a line starts with @. Producer metadata is needed when historical encoding is ambiguous.

blocks.text: Canonical BEDv1 describes 0-based half-open intervals. The first three fields are chromosome, start and end. sections.title: Distinguish feature relationships and coding phase

blocks.text: A gene can have transcripts; a transcript can contain exons. Exons are retained in mature RNA and can include untranslated regions, so exon does not mean entirely protein-coding. CDS is the portion used to encode protein. A codon is a three-base unit. For a CDS row, phase 0, 1 or 2 tells how many bases to move from that row’s 5′ end to the 5′ genomic coordinate of the next complete codon, rather than necessarily its lower genomic endpoint. On + the 5′ end is the lower coordinate; on − it is the higher coordinate and movement proceeds toward lower coordinates. Phase is not genomic coordinate modulo 3. These are annotation rules, not evidence that a prediction is biologically correct.

blocks.text: GFF3 is a distinct nine-column grammar, with a required topmost ##gff-version 3 directive and unquoted tag=value attributes separated by semicolons. sections.title: Account for query and reference consumption

blocks.text: An alignment relates a query/read sequence to a reference. CIGAR contains length/operator pairs. M, = and X consume both query and reference; M alone does not distinguish a match from a mismatch. I and S consume query only; D and N consume reference only; H and P consume neither. If SEQ is present, its length must equal query-consuming CIGAR lengths when CIGAR is available. With a nonzero mapped POS, the last ordinary covered reference coordinate is POS + reference-consumed length − 1. Missing values and unmapped records have their own rules; this shortcut is for the explicitly mapped examples.

source_refs.locator: §1.4: FLAG, POS, MAPQ, CIGAR, SEQ and QUAL

blocks.text: Flags are bit fields. In the supplied examples FLAG=0 is an unpaired mapped record; bit 4 indicates unmapped. A nonzero flag is not inherently invalid, and an unmapped record may still be placed on a reference. MAPQ is mapping confidence; 255 means unavailable, not maximum confidence. QUAL is per-base quality or * for unavailable. If a non-* SEQ and QUAL are supplied, their lengths must agree.

sections.title: Distinguish alignment text from binary containers

blocks.text: SAM is alignment text. Optional header rows precede records; @SQ gives reference SN (name) and LN (length). A record has at least eleven tab-separated fields: QNAME FLAG RNAME POS MAPQ CIGAR RNEXT PNEXT TLEN SEQ QUAL. POS is 1-based in ordinary mapped records. Extra tags use TAG:TYPE:VALUE. Headers, flags, missing markers and supplied reference context must be interpreted together; optional unavailable CIGAR or QUAL is not universally an error. Sorting, an index or a particular producer’s read-group policy is not a universal requirement for every valid SAM file.

blocks.text: BAM represents SAM alignment data in a BGZF-compressed binary container. The magic BAM\x01 is at the start of the decompressed BAM stream, not the outer on-disk compressed bytes. A text preview produced by decoding is SAM output, not proof that the original container was plain SAM. BAM stores reference offsets internally as 0-based values while a SAM rendering uses its specified 1-based POS. A compatible parser establishes container type more strongly than a filename. Header/EOF checks, full restoration and semantic validation provide different evidence.

sections.title: Separate variant rows from reference-confidence blocks

blocks.text: VCF begins with ##fileformat metadata and a #CHROM header. Its eight fixed columns are CHROM POS ID REF ALT QUAL FILTER INFO; optional FORMAT and sample columns follow. Tabs delimit fields. Missing values use . rather than an empty field. Ordinary POS is 1-based, with specific telomeric exceptions outside our examples. Header definitions declare INFO/FORMAT type and cardinality: Number=A means one value per ALT; Number=R means one per REF plus ALTs; Number=G depends on genotype combinations/ploidy. GT indexes must exist. FILTER=PASS means applied filters passed; . means filters were not applied, not automatic success. REF agreement requires the exact matching reference.
